4047.title: Minimum Operations to Make XOR of All Elements Zero
4047.explanationMarkdown:
Let `T` be the XOR of the entire array. If `T = 0`, the answer is already zero. If every element has the same value and `T != 0`, no legal operation exists: the operation requires two unequal values.

For the remaining cases, find the fewest original values whose XOR is `T`. Treat each possible XOR value as a graph vertex. From a vertex `x`, using an original value `v` gives an edge to `x ^ v`. Every edge costs one, so an unweighted shortest path from `0` to `T` gives the minimum number `m` of selected values. Repeated occurrences of the same value are unnecessary in a shortest path because using a value twice cancels it.

The implementation builds the set of distinct values and uses bidirectional BFS. The two frontier sets start at `0` and `T`; XOR edges are reversible, so either side can be expanded. Expand the smaller frontier, record the expanded states, and form the next layer by XORing with each distinct original value. When the frontiers intersect, the number of expanded layers is their shortest-path distance. The second implementation performs ordinary BFS over the same graph.

Why does this graph distance equal the operation count? A useful lower bound comes from tracking which original elements contribute to the final total. Initially the total uses every original element once. Read a sequence of XOR replacements backward: each replacement changes at most one coefficient in this representation. Therefore, after `k` operations, at most `k` original indices can have been removed from the total. If the final total is zero, those removed elements XOR to `T`, so `k >= m`.

For achievability, suppose a minimum subset `S` with XOR `T` leaves at least one original index outside it. Keep the elements of `S` unchanged as donors and choose an outside element as a receiver whose value is not `T`. Such a receiver exists: if `m > 1`, no original value can equal `T`; if `m = 1`, the earlier unequal-values check guarantees another value. XOR every donor into that receiver. The total changes by exactly `T` and becomes zero. The donors have distinct values. While at least two remain, at most one can equal the receiver, so another legal donor can be chosen. The last donor cannot equal the receiver because the receiver's eventual value is its original value XOR `T`, which is nonzero. Thus exactly `m` legal operations suffice.

If `m = n`, where `n` is the array length, the only subset with XOR `T` is the whole array. Equivalently, no nonempty subset of the original values has XOR zero. XOR replacements are invertible linear operations on these values, so they cannot create a zero XOR of all elements in this case. Return `-1`, which explains the final `steps != nums.size()` check.

For example, `[1,2,4]` needs all three original values to represent `T = 7`, so it is impossible. Duplicate values can instead leave a zero-XOR subset available. Always handle `T = 0` before the all-equal check: an even number of equal elements already has total zero.
4047.timeComplexity: Expected O(n + U*d), where n is the array length, d is the number of distinct values, b = bit_width(max(nums)), and U = 2^b. Each of at most U XOR states considers d edges. Since U <= 2*max(nums), this is also O(n + max(nums)*d). Hash-set operations are expected constant time.
4047.spaceComplexity: O(U + d) auxiliary space for visited states, BFS frontiers, and distinct values. Here nums[i] <= 2000, so U <= 2048.
checks: Executed the supplied primary Python algorithm, which matches the C++ bidirectional BFS, against an independent graph of actual legal array operations.
All 1,708 multisets of lengths 2 through 6 over values 1 through 7 matched exact shortest distances from a multi-source BFS starting at all zero-XOR arrays.
The exhaustive cases include already-zero totals, all-equal arrays, duplicate donors, linearly independent values, and reachable targets requiring multiple operations.

4054.title: Count Shadow Pairs I
4054.explanationMarkdown:
Scan the array from left to right, treating the current position as the right endpoint `j`. An earlier index `i` remains a possible left endpoint only until a strictly smaller value appears after it. Once that happens, the smaller value is permanently between `i` and every future endpoint, so `i` can never form another shadow pair.

Keep these still-eligible earlier values in `stk`, in nondecreasing order. Maintain `cnt[v]`, the number of occurrences of value `v` currently in the stack. For each current value `x`:

1. Pop every stack value greater than `x`, decrementing its frequency. None can form a pair with `x`, and `x` blocks it for all future endpoints.
2. Every remaining stack value is at most `x`. All values strictly below `x` form a valid pair ending here; equal values fail the required strict inequality. Add `stk.size() - cnt[x]` to the answer.
3. Push `x` and increment `cnt[x]` so this occurrence can serve as a future left endpoint.

The invariant is exact: a retained occurrence has no strictly smaller value between its index and the current position. A popped occurrence has a witnessed blocker. Consequently the second step counts every valid left endpoint once, and processing each right endpoint counts every shadow pair exactly once.

Equal values must stay in the stack. They do not block one another, although they cannot pair with each other. This is why the pop condition is `>` rather than `>=`, and why equal frequencies are subtracted from the contribution.

For `[3,1,4,1,5]`, the value `1` removes the earlier `3`. The `4` pairs with one retained `1`; the next `1` removes `4` but preserves the first `1`; finally `5` pairs with both retained ones, giving three pairs. Use a 64-bit answer: with `n = 100000`, a strictly increasing array has `n*(n-1)/2` pairs, which exceeds a 32-bit signed integer.
4054.timeComplexity: Expected O(n). Each occurrence is pushed once and popped at most once, and each frequency-table operation has expected O(1) cost.
4054.spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the stack and frequency table.
checks: All 21,824 arrays of lengths 3 through 7 over values 1 through 4 matched a direct oracle that enumerates each pair and every intervening potential blocker.
This includes all-equal, increasing, decreasing, repeated-minimum, and mixed arrays.

4055.title: Count Shadow Pairs II
4055.explanationMarkdown:
Here a blocker must have a value strictly between the two endpoint values. The supplied solution divides by value, not by array position. Compress the distinct values into sorted ranks, and create one group per value containing its occurrence indices in increasing order. Repeatedly merge adjacent groups. Each merged pair represents a lower value range and a strictly higher value range.

A pair with unequal endpoint values is considered at exactly one merge: the merge where its two value groups first meet. All values strictly between those endpoints also belong to that merged range. Values outside the range cannot block the pair, so counting cross-range pairs at this merge is sufficient. Equal endpoint values begin in the same group and are never counted as cross-range pairs.

During `merge_and_count(left, right)`, both lists contain indices sorted by position. Scan the right-list indices `j` in order, inserting all lower-range indices `i < j` before counting pairs ending at `j`. Two stacks maintain the blockers:

- `stk1` stores the surviving lower-range left endpoints, in index order and with nonincreasing values. When a new lower-range value `y` arrives, pop smaller values from its end. Each popped endpoint now has `y` after it, and `y` lies below every higher-range right endpoint, so `y` permanently blocks that endpoint in this merge. Equal values are retained because a blocker must be strictly larger than the left endpoint.
- `stk2` stores earlier higher-range values in strictly increasing order, together with a boundary into `stk1`. For a current right value `x`, discard stack entries with value `>= x`: those values cannot lie strictly below `x`. If an entry remains, its top represents the latest relevant higher-range blocker with value below `x`. Every surviving lower-range candidate before that blocker is invalid; candidates after it remain valid.

The integer stored with a `stk2` entry is the length of the blocked prefix of `stk1`. When `stk1` shrinks, this boundary may also shrink, so the code clamps the top boundary with `min(boundary, stk1.size())`. When a `stk2` entry is popped, its possibly reduced boundary is propagated to the next entry using another minimum. This lazy propagation keeps the active blocked-prefix length correct without rescanning either stack.

The contribution for a right endpoint is therefore `stk1.size() - blockedPrefix`, using zero when no higher-range blocker remains. Then push the current right value with the current `stk1` length as its boundary. Meanwhile, merge the original indices into a sorted list so the next value-range merge can use the same procedure.

Why are these tests sufficient? A value strictly between the endpoints belongs either to the lower range or the higher range. Lower-range blockers are exactly what the `stk1` removals eliminate. Among higher-range blockers, the latest one invalidates a prefix of the remaining candidates, exactly what `stk2` measures. A counted candidate has neither kind of blocker, and every rejected candidate has at least one.

All-equal arrays have only one initial value group and return zero immediately. Keep both strictness rules as written: `stk1` pops `< y`, while `stk2` pops `>= x`. Under the constraint `n <= 50000`, even the bound `n*(n-1)/2` fits the implementation's signed 32-bit return type.
4055.timeComplexity: Expected O(n log n): sorting for coordinate compression costs O(n log n), and the bottom-up merging costs O(n log d), where d is the number of distinct values. Each stack entry is pushed and popped at most once per merge level. Rank hash-table operations are expected O(1).
4055.spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for compressed value groups, merged index lists, and the two stacks. Old and new merge levels together contain only O(n) indices.
checks: All 21,824 arrays of lengths 3 through 7 over values 1 through 4 matched a direct oracle that checks nums[i] < nums[j] and searches every intervening value for nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j].
Executed the supplied Python implementation with xrange mapped to range; its stack and merge operations match the supplied C++ algorithm.

4058.title: Maximum Pulse Value After One Subarray Rotation
4058.explanationMarkdown:
Write `b[i] = nums[i]` for even indices and `b[i] = -nums[i]` for odd indices. The original pulse is the sum of `b`.

A left rotation moves every element except the first one position to the left, flipping its contribution's sign. If the rotated subarray has even length, its first element also changes index parity, so the whole subarray's signed sum is negated. If it has odd length, its first element keeps its sign, and only the remaining even-length suffix is negated. Thus every possible gain is `-2 * S`, where `S` is the signed sum of some even-length contiguous subarray. Conversely, every even-length subarray can itself be rotated to achieve that gain.

The problem is therefore to find the minimum even-length subarray sum in `b`, or use zero if skipping the operation is better. Let `P[t]` be the sum of the first `t` signed values. An interval `[l,r]` has even length exactly when `l` and `r+1` have the same parity, and its signed sum is `P[r+1] - P[l]`.

Scan from left to right while maintaining `prefix = P[i+1]`. To minimize a difference ending at the current position, subtract the largest earlier prefix with the same prefix-length parity. The code stores these two maxima in `lookup`, indexed by the parity of the prefix's ending array index. Its initial values are `[-infinity, 0]`: the empty prefix ends at the conceptual index `-1`, which belongs to the odd bucket.

At each index `i`, first add its signed value to `prefix`. If `lookup[i % 2]` exists, use `prefix - lookup[i % 2]` to update `mn`, the smallest eligible subarray sum seen so far. Then update that lookup bucket with the new maximum prefix. Querying before updating uses an earlier prefix and therefore a nonempty even-length interval. Initializing `mn = 0` separately includes the option of doing nothing.

After the scan, `prefix` is the original pulse and the answer is `prefix - 2*mn`. This considers every even-length interval through its right endpoint and chooses the largest achievable gain, which proves optimality.

Negative numbers need no special handling: the parity transformation and prefix differences still apply. For an array of length one, no eligible interval exists, so the original pulse is returned. The C++ version uses 64-bit sums because up to 100000 values of magnitude 10^9 can contribute.
4058.timeComplexity: O(n): one pass with constant work per element.
4058.spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: one running prefix, one minimum, and two prefix maxima.
checks: All 19,530 arrays of lengths 1 through 6 over values −2 through 2 matched an oracle that explicitly constructs every legal one-position left rotation and also checks no operation.
The exhaustive comparison includes negative values, zeros, single-element arrays, and cases where no rotation improves the pulse.
Algebraically reduced both even- and odd-length rotations to sign reversal of an even-length signed interval.

4059.title: Lexicographically Largest Power Array
4059.explanationMarkdown:
The entry for bit 14 has priority over every later entry, then bit 13 has priority over the remaining ones, and so on. Optimize the bits in that order while preserving every earlier prefix length.

Maintain an ordered list of groups. Elements may still be rearranged freely inside a group, while the established group order records the constraints imposed by previously optimized bits. Initially all elements are in one group.

For the current bit, scan these groups from the beginning:

1. If a group consists entirely of elements with this bit set, every element in it can extend the current all-one prefix. Add its size and continue.
2. At the first group that contains a zero in this bit, collect its one-bit elements. Put all of them first and add their count to the prefix length. If both kinds exist, replace the group by a one-bit group followed by a zero-bit group.
3. Stop at this first zero-containing group. It necessarily ends the prefix; changing any later group cannot improve this entry. Leave the later groups unrestricted for future, lower-priority bits.

Store the resulting prefix length in `result[14 - bit]`. If the scan reaches the end, all `n` elements have this bit set and the entry is `n`. If the first group has no one-bit element, the entry is zero and no split is necessary.

The greedy choice is optimal by induction on the processed bits. Before a bit is processed, rearrangements inside the current groups preserve all earlier entries. All fully one-bit groups must contribute their entire sizes. Within the first group containing a zero, no arrangement can extend the prefix past all of that group's one-bit elements, since a zero must then appear. Placing every one-bit element first achieves this upper bound. Splitting only that group retains the needed ordering and preserves all remaining freedom. Consequently the current entry is maximized subject to the already-optimal earlier entries, which is exactly lexicographic maximization.

Do not sort or partition every group for each bit. A group after the first zero does not affect the current entry, and imposing extra ordering there can harm a later entry. For example, in `[10,11,5,3]`, bit 3 first fixes the two values 10 and 11 ahead of 5 and 3. Bit 2 then has prefix length zero. For bit 1, putting 3 ahead of 5 extends the prefix to three; ordinary descending numeric order would unnecessarily keep 5 first and obtain only two.

Zeros, duplicate values, and bits absent from every element all follow the same rules. The algorithm needs only the prefix lengths, so it never has to assemble a final permutation.
4059.timeComplexity: O(L*n) with L = 15, hence O(n) for the stated bit width. Each bit scans and partitions at most n elements. At most one group is split per bit; vector insertion moves at most min(n, L+1) group objects and is also covered by O(L*n).
4059.spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the ordered groups and temporary partitions; their live element storage is linear. The returned array has L = 15 entries.
